title: Tax on Nigerian Stocks: What NGX Investors Need to Know
summary: How dividends and capital gains on NGX shares are taxed in Nigeria, including the 2026 changes and the exemption that covers most small investors.
body_markdown:
**In short:** Two taxes apply to NGX shares: a 10% withholding tax on dividends, deducted at source as a final tax, and capital gains tax when you sell. Since 2026, gains are taxed at your income tax band, but most retail investors are exempt, because gains under ₦10 million and proceeds under ₦150 million in a year are not taxed.


Tax is the part of investing that makes people freeze. Ask around and you will hear that the Nigerian stock market is taxed at 30%, or that the taxman takes a cut every time you sell. Most of this is either out of date or simply wrong, and the confusion has only grown since Nigeria overhauled its tax laws.


This guide explains, in plain terms, how investing in shares on the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) is actually taxed: the tax on your dividends, the tax on your gains when you sell, and the 2026 changes that matter most to you. It is general information rather than tax advice, and because the rules are new, we point you to the sources and recommend confirming your own position with a professional.


If you are still getting to grips with how NGX investing works in the first place, our[complete guide to investing in the Nigerian stock market](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-invest-in-the-nigerian-stock-market-ngx-a-complete-beginners-guide/) covers the basics. This article picks up where tax is concerned.


## Do you pay tax on Nigerian stocks?


Yes, but for most everyday investors the amount is small, and many pay no capital gains tax at all. Two taxes matter when you invest in NGX shares: a withholding tax on the dividends you receive, and capital gains tax on the profit you make when you sell. We take each in turn.


The headline most people miss is that Nigeria’s 2026 tax reform made the system more generous to small investors, not less. The widely repeated belief that share profits are taxed at a flat 30% is no longer how it works, and for many investors was never quite right to begin with.


## Tax on dividends


[Dividends from Nigerian shares](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-dividends-work-for-investors-on-the-nigerian-stock-exchange/) are subject to a withholding tax of 10%, which is deducted before the money reaches you.


In practice, you do not calculate or pay this yourself. When a company pays a dividend, the tax is withheld at source, and the amount that lands in your account is already net of it. For most individual investors, this withholding tax is[treated as a final tax](https://doclib.ngxgroup.com/investors-site/becoming-an-investor/FAQs/Applicable%20Taxes%20for%20Investors%20and%20Issuers%20on%20Capital%20Market%20Transactions.pdf) , which means there is nothing further to do and nothing more to pay on that dividend.


If you are taxed in a country that has a double taxation treaty with Nigeria, the rate may be reduced, commonly to 7.5%.


On[Bamboo](https://investbamboo.com/nigerian-stocks) , the dividends credited to your account are already net of this withholding tax, so the amount you see is what you keep, without any deduction to manage yourself.


## Capital gains tax: what changed in 2026


The biggest change is that the old flat 10% capital gains tax is gone. From 1 January 2026, under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, gains on shares are taxed at your personal income tax rate rather than at a single flat rate.


As[PwC’s summary of the reform sets out](https://www.pwc.com/ng/en/publications/the-nigerian-tax-reform-acts.html) , capital gains have been folded into the income tax system. For individuals, that means your gains are added to your other income and taxed at the progressive personal income tax rates, which run from 0% up to 25%. Companies are taxed on gains at the corporate rate, generally 30%.


What this means in practice depends on your income. A lower earner may pay little or nothing on a modest gain, while a high earner realising a large gain could pay more than the old flat rate would have cost. The system is now progressive: the more you earn overall, the higher the rate that applies to your gains. For the typical retail investor, as the next section explains, the more important point is that an exemption usually applies before any rate even comes into play.


## The exemption that covers most investors


Most retail investors are exempt from capital gains tax on shares, because the law exempts gains that fall below two thresholds. You are exempt when your total proceeds from selling shares do not exceed ₦150 million in a twelve-month period, and your total gains do not exceed ₦10 million in that same period.


Both conditions matter, and this is where people get caught out. As[reporting on the new rules explains](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/top-news/834728-what-you-need-to-know-about-the-new-capital-gains-tax-rules.html) , if you cross either threshold, your gains become taxable. To make that concrete: sell shares worth ₦80 million for a ₦6 million gain and you are within both limits, so you pay nothing. Sell shares worth ₦200 million for an ₦8 million gain and, even though your gain is under ₦10 million, your proceeds are over ₦150 million, so the gain becomes taxable at your income tax band.


For the large majority of individual investors, these thresholds are generous enough that no capital gains tax applies at all. The chairman of the presidential committee on tax reform has[made the same point publicly](https://www.tv360nigeria.com/2026-tax-reform-small-investors-exempt-from-capital-gains-tax-oyedele/) , noting that most small investors are fully exempt and that the belief the market is taxed at 30% is simply a misunderstanding. If your investing is at the scale most Nigerians invest at, capital gains tax is unlikely to touch you.


## What about shares you already owned?


If you held shares before 2026, the new rules do not reach back to tax gains you had already built up. For existing investments, the cost base is reset to the higher of what you actually paid and the closing market price on 31 December 2025.


In plain terms, only the growth from the start of 2026 onward counts toward a taxable gain. Gains that accrued before then are grandfathered. This matters if you have held a stock for years, because it means you are not suddenly taxed on a long stretch of appreciation the moment you sell after the new rules begin.


## Reinvestment relief


If your share sales do go over the exemption thresholds, there is still relief available if you put the money back to work. Where you reinvest the proceeds into shares of other Nigerian companies within twelve months, the reinvested portion can qualify for exemption. The rule rewards investors who keep their capital in the market rather than taking it off the table, and it is worth knowing about if you are ever managing a larger portfolio.


## If you invest from abroad


The dividend withholding tax applies whether you live in Nigeria or abroad, and the rate may be lower if your country has a tax treaty with Nigeria. On top of that, you may have tax obligations where you live, and those depend entirely on your country’s own rules. If you are investing from the diaspora, our[guide to investing in the NGX from abroad](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-nigerians-abroad-can-invest-in-ngx-stocks/) covers the accounts and the process, and you should speak to a tax professional in your country of residence about your personal position.


## Keeping records and staying compliant


Even if you expect to be exempt, keep good records. Hold on to documentation of what you paid for your shares, what you sold them for, the dates involved, and any related costs such as brokerage fees, which can be deducted when working out a gain.


If you do cross the thresholds, capital gains are reported and paid through the tax system, with deadlines and forms set by the tax authorities. This is where mistakes get expensive, so it is worth getting advice rather than guessing, especially in this first year under the new rules while everyone, including the authorities, settles into them.


## Frequently asked questions


**Do I pay tax when I buy Nigerian shares?** No. Tax does not arise when you buy. It arises on the dividends you receive and on the gains you make when you sell, and even then an exemption covers most individual investors.


**How much tax do I pay on dividends?** Dividends are subject to a withholding tax, deducted before the money reaches you, and for most individuals this is a final tax with nothing further to pay. The rate may be reduced if you are covered by a tax treaty.


**Is there still a flat 10% capital gains tax on shares?** No. From 1 January 2026, the flat rate was replaced. Gains are now taxed at your personal income tax band, which for individuals runs from 0% to 25%.


**Am I exempt from capital gains tax on shares?** You are exempt if your total share-sale proceeds are within ₦150 million and your total gains are within ₦10 million over a twelve-month period. Cross either threshold and your gains become taxable. Most retail investors fall within the exemption.


**Will I be taxed on gains from before 2026?** No. For shares held before 2026, the cost base is reset to the higher of your purchase price or the 31 December 2025 market price, so gains built up before the new rules are not caught.


**Do diaspora investors pay Nigerian tax on shares?** The dividend withholding tax applies, potentially at a reduced treaty rate, and you may also owe tax where you live. Speak to a tax professional about your specific situation.


---


**Important:** This article is for general educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, financial, or investment advice. Tax treatment depends on your individual circumstances and can change. The rules described here took effect on 1 January 2026 and are still settling, so confirm your position with a qualified tax professional before acting. Investing carries risk, the value of investments can go down as well as up, and dividends are not guaranteed.

### Quick Summary


This guide explains how investing in Nigerian stocks (NGX shares) is taxed. Dividends are subject to a 10% withholding tax, reduced to 7.5% for treaty countries, deducted at source and treated as a final tax for most individual investors. Capital gains tax changed on 1 January 2026 under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025: the old flat 10% rate was replaced, and gains are now taxed at personal income tax rates of 0% to 25% for individuals. Most retail investors are exempt, because gains are not taxed where total proceeds do not exceed ₦150 million and total gains do not exceed ₦10 million in a 12-month period. This is general information, not tax advice.
